Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 96, verse 6–19:

"Nay!" (kalla) is a rebuke to the one who disbelieved in the blessing of God upon him through his transgression. Although it is not mentioned, the context indicates it: "That he saw himself" (an ra'ahu an ra'a nafsahu). It is said of the verbs of the heart: "I saw myself" (ra'aytunī) and "I knew myself" ('alimtunī), and that is one of their particular features. The meaning of "seeing" (al-ru'ya) here is knowledge; if it meant sight (al-ibsar), the combination of the two pronouns with its verb would be impossible. "Independence" (istaghna) is the second object, and "Indeed, to your Lord is the return" (inna ila rabbika al-ruj'a) is in the manner of a shift (iltifat) to address the human being, as a threat to him and a warning about the consequence of transgression. Al-ruj'a is a verbal noun like al-bushra, meaning "return."

It has been said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, and likewise "Have you seen the one who forbids" (ara'ayta alladhi yanha). It is narrated that he said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Do you claim that whoever is independent transgresses? Then make the mountains of Mecca silver and gold for us, that we may take from them and then transgress, and abandon our religion and follow your religion." Then Gabriel came down and said: "If you wish, We will do that, but if they do not believe, We will do to them what We did to the people of the table (ashab al-ma'ida)." So the Messenger of God ﷺ refrained from calling them, out of mercy toward them. [[I have not found it. I say: its ending has preceded in al-Isra' in a different context.]] It is also narrated from him, may God curse him, that he said: "Does Muhammad rub his face in the dust among you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "By Him by whom I swear, if I see him, I will trample his neck." Then he came to him, and then turned back on his heels, and they said to him: "What is wrong with you, O Abu al-Hakam?" He said: "Between me and him is a trench of fire, and horror, and wings." Then "Have you seen the one who forbids" was revealed.

Its meaning: Tell me about the one who forbids some of God's servants from their prayer, if that forbidding one is upon a sound course in what he forbids of the worship of God, or if he is commanding righteousness and piety in what he commands of the worship of idols, as he believes, and likewise if he is one who denies the truth and turns away from the correct religion, as we say. "Does he not know that God sees" and observes his states, of guidance and misguidance, and will recompense him according to that. This is a threat.

If you ask: what is the object of "have you seen" (ara'ayta)? I say: "the one who forbids" together with the conditional clause, and they are in the position of the two objects. If you ask: where is the answer of the condition? I say: it is omitted, its estimate being: "If he is upon guidance or commands piety, does he not know that God sees?" It was omitted because its mention is indicated by the answer of the second condition. If you ask: how is it correct that "Does he not know" be the answer of the condition? I say: as it is correct in your saying: "If I honor you, will you honor me?" and "If Zayd does good to you, will you do good to him?" If you ask: what is the second "ara'ayta" and its placement between the objects of "ara'ayta"? I say: it is superfluous, repeated for emphasis.

It is related from al-Hasan that it was Umayya ibn Khalaf who used to forbid Salman from prayer. "Nay!" is a rebuke to Abu Jahl and a repudiation of him for forbidding the worship of God, the Exalted, and for commanding the worship of al-Lat. Then He said: "If he does not desist from what he is in, We will surely seize him by the forelock" (lanasfa'an bi'l-nasiya), meaning: We will surely take hold of his forelock and drag him by it into the Fire.

Al-safʿ means seizing a thing and pulling it with force. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said:

"A people who, when the cry (al-sarikh) comes, you see them
between one who bridles his horse and one who seizes it [[By Humayd ibn Thawr al-Hilali, the Companion. That is: they are a people who, when the cry rises, that is, the shouting for war, hasten to it, so you see them moving between one who bridles his horse and one who seizes, that is, one who grasps its forelock and pulls it toward him swiftly. "Min" is superfluous, and it would be so even in affirmative speech. "Aw" means "wa." It is also narrated as "idha yaqa'" with a ya', meaning: occurs. It is also narrated as "idha hatafa," meaning: shouted, so it is like "jadd jaddu-hu." It is permissible that "al-sarikh" means "al-sarikh" (one who cries). It is narrated as "idha sami'u al-sarikh," then it is the object. It is narrated as "ma bayna mulajjim."

This supports that "min" in that narration is superfluous.]]"

It is read "la-nasfa'anna" with a doubled nun. Ibn Mas'ud read "la-asfa'an." I wrote it in the Mushaf with an alif according to the rule of pausal reading. Since it is known that it is the forelock of the one mentioned, he dispensed with the definite article's reference by the "lam of 'ahd" instead of the annexation. "Nasiya" (forelock) is in apposition to "al-nasiya," and it is permissible for an indefinite to be substituted for a definite here because it is qualified, so it stands by itself with a benefit. It is read "nasiyatun," on the basis of "hiya nasiyatun" (it is a forelock). And "nasiyata" in the accusative. Both are for insult.

He described it with lying and error by metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), though in reality they belong to its owner. In it is a beauty and eloquence that is absent from your saying "a lying, erring forelock." "Al-nadi" is the assembly where people gather, that is, they meet. The intended meaning is "the people of the assembly," as Jarir said:

"For them is an assembly, tawny of mustaches, humbled [among themselves],
mighty against whoever opposes them, so know this."

He says: they have an assembly where they gather, or they have people gathered and seated, and you do not see that except among chiefs and nobles. "Sahab" (tawny) for "al-sibal" (mustaches) is an adjective of the referent of the pronoun in "lahum" according to the first reading, and an adjective of "majlis" according to the second, because it means "those sitting." "Al-sahba" is a redness overlaying blackness. "Al-sahab" is the plural of "asfar"... [the plural of "aṣhab"]. "Al-sal" is the edge of the mustache beside the mouth, and that tawniness is a characteristic of the Byzantines, and it is a metaphor for harshness and severity. "Adhilla" means: among themselves they are humble, and against those who oppose them they are mighty. The object was placed first for restriction, so know this and be certain of it, for it is true. It is narrated instead of the second half:

"Equal, their free and their slaves."

"Sawasiyya" is like "tawa'iyya," the plural of "sawa'" by non-analogical formation. It is said: it is a collective noun meaning "equal." That is: they are equal in nobility and perfection of character. Were it not for the context of praise, it would be of the type of "tawjih," since it allows also a sense of blame. As for reading it with kasra and tashdid, it is a nisba to "al-sawwas," which is training in good conduct; meaning that all of them are chiefs. But the first is more apt. And from the hadith: "People are equal; no Arab has merit over a non-Arab except through piety," as in the commentary translation of Sharh al-Qamus.

And Zuhayr said:

"Among them are stations, their faces are handsome,"

and "al-maqama" is the assembly.

It is related that Abu Jahl passed by the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was praying, and said: "Did I not forbid you?" The Messenger of God ﷺ spoke harshly to him, and he said: "Do you threaten me, when I am the most numerous of the people of the valley in assembly?" Then it was revealed. Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "sa-yad'u al-zabaniya" with the passive voice of the verb. In the speech of the Arabs, "al-zabaniya" are the police (al-shurta); the singular is "zabaniya," like "'ifriya," from "al-zabn," which is pushing. It is said: "zabanaa," as if it were attributed to "al-zabn," then altered for the relative form, as in the saying "amsa." Its origin is "zabani," then it was said "zabaniya" by compensation. "Do not obey him" (la tuti'hu), that is: remain upon what you are upon of disobedience to him, as in His saying: "So do not obey the deniers" (fa la tuti'i al-mukadhdhibin). Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 96, verse 6–19:

"Nay!" (kalla) is a rebuke to the one who disbelieved in the blessing of God upon him through his transgression. Although it is not mentioned, the context indicates it: "That he saw himself" (an ra'ahu an ra'a nafsahu). It is said of the verbs of the heart: "I saw myself" (ra'aytunī) and "I knew myself" ('alimtunī), and that is one of their particular features. The meaning of "seeing" (al-ru'ya) here is knowledge; if it meant sight (al-ibsar), the combination of the two pronouns with its verb would be impossible. "Independence" (istaghna) is the second object, and "Indeed, to your Lord is the return" (inna ila rabbika al-ruj'a) is in the manner of a shift (iltifat) to address the human being, as a threat to him and a warning about the consequence of transgression. Al-ruj'a is a verbal noun like al-bushra, meaning "return."

It has been said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, and likewise "Have you seen the one who forbids" (ara'ayta alladhi yanha). It is narrated that he said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Do you claim that whoever is independent transgresses? Then make the mountains of Mecca silver and gold for us, that we may take from them and then transgress, and abandon our religion and follow your religion." Then Gabriel came down and said: "If you wish, We will do that, but if they do not believe, We will do to them what We did to the people of the table (ashab al-ma'ida)." So the Messenger of God ﷺ refrained from calling them, out of mercy toward them. [[I have not found it. I say: its ending has preceded in al-Isra' in a different context.]] It is also narrated from him, may God curse him, that he said: "Does Muhammad rub his face in the dust among you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "By Him by whom I swear, if I see him, I will trample his neck." Then he came to him, and then turned back on his heels, and they said to him: "What is wrong with you, O Abu al-Hakam?" He said: "Between me and him is a trench of fire, and horror, and wings." Its meaning: Tell me about the one who forbids some of God's servants from their prayer, if that forbidding one is upon a sound course in what he forbids of the worship of God, or if he is commanding righteousness and piety in what he commands of the worship of idols, as he believes, and likewise if he is one who denies the truth and turns away from the correct religion, as we say. If you ask: where is the answer of the condition? I say: it is omitted, its estimate being: "If he is upon guidance or commands piety, does he not know that God sees?" It was omitted because its mention is indicated by the answer of the second condition. If you ask: how is it correct that "Does he not know" be the answer of the condition? I say: as it is correct in your saying: "If I honor you, will you honor me?" and "If Zayd does good to you, will you do good to him?" If you ask: what is the second "ara'ayta" and its placement between the objects of "ara'ayta"? I say: it is superfluous, repeated for emphasis.

It is related from al-Hasan that it was Umayya ibn Khalaf who used to forbid Salman from prayer. "Nay!" is a rebuke to Abu Jahl and a repudiation of him for forbidding the worship of God, the Exalted, and for commanding the worship of al-Lat. Then He said: "If he does not desist from what he is in, We will surely seize him by the forelock" (lanasfa'an bi'l-nasiya), meaning: We will surely take hold of his forelock and drag him by it into the Fire.

Al-safʿ means seizing a thing and pulling it with force. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said:

between one who bridles his horse and one who seizes it [[By Humayd ibn Thawr al-Hilali, the Companion.
